title: Ghoul! Chewer of corpses!
html_source:
The word “ghoul” comes from Arabian mythology (Arabic: غُول, or ghūl) where it is a demon or monster that does precisely what Stephen says: eats corpses. It often takes the forms of animals, especially the hyena, or the form of the dead person whose body it ate last. Arabian ghoul imagery reappears a few times in chapter 15, “Circe”: a dog eats the remains of Paddy Dignam (whose funeral we saw in chapter 6, “Hades”) and takes the form of his partially “ghouleaten” body; then later Stephen has a vision of his mother rising from the grave, which he once again declares is “The ghoul!”, “The corpsechewer!” and “Hyena!”

The concept of the Ghoul was introduced to western culture via translations of One Thousand and One Nights (aka “Arabian Nights”), which are alluded to many times throughout Ulysses.
